introduction: “Close your eyes to racial differences, and welcome all with the light of oneness.” The guide opens there and returns to it in talks and letters, most of them ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s to Americans around 1912: colour is accidental and the heart is judged; the hatred between black and white will end in bloodshed if it is not healed; let the two races meet, eat, sing, marry and work together until “the names of black and white shall vanish”. The oldest company for this is scriptural: one blood, one Father, a God who is no respecter of persons and looks on the heart, nations and tribes made that they may know one another. The nearest company is American, and it argues. Lincoln and Jefferson feared the same reckoning; Harlan called the Constitution colour-blind; King dreamed of the table of brotherhood. Douglass says that power concedes nothing without a demand and that the country’s Christianity had blessed the lash; Du Bois describes two souls in one dark body; Booker T. Washington proposes to stay separate as the fingers; Hughes is sent to eat in the kitchen. Blake, Kipling and Ezra show how old and how respectable the opposite assumptions are.
questions: Samuel is told that the Lord looks on the heart, and King asks that his children be judged by the content of their character. What do the readings add to these by their images of the pupil of the eye, the doves and the garden?
The Qur’an counts the difference of colours among God’s signs, while several readings ask us to close our eyes to it. Is there a difference between not seeing colour and seeing it as a sign?
Zangwill’s melting pot, Kallen’s orchestra and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s bouquet of violets are three pictures of one country. What does each keep and what does each give up?

Douglass holds that there is no progress without struggle and demand; the readings say the enmity “cannot be effaced except through” love and faith. Are these rivals, or do they answer different questions?

Booker T. Washington offered separation in “all things purely social”; the readings ask for shared meetings, homes and marriages. Why do they treat the social as the place where the matter is decided?
Ruth is welcomed and Ezra sends the foreign wives away. What does the guide’s praise of marriage between races ask of a community that the story of Othello shows it may not be ready to give?

outside.why: “Close your eyes to racial differences.” The Qur’an counts the difference of languages and colours among the signs of God, beside the creation of the heavens and the earth: not closed eyes there, but eyes opened to a wonder.
The pupil of the eye is black and the source of light. The bride of the Song says of herself, “I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem”.
“God has made all mankind of one family.” Paul tells Athens that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men”.

No race is superior to another. The nations wrote it into their Declaration of 1948: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.
“Do not mistrust them and withdraw yourself.” Leviticus commands of the stranger: he shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself.
“Sons of the same Father.” Malachi’s question to a quarrelling people: have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?
“Let it be known by your behaviour that you are indeed the people of God.” The same test in John: by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
In the Kingdom “the heart and soul are considered”. When Samuel is choosing a king he is told: man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
Martin Luther King’s dream for his four children is this reading in an American voice: a nation where they are judged not by the colour of their skin but by the content of their character.
“Color is not the standard and estimate of judgment.” Jesus to the crowd: judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
The reading uses Peter’s own phrase. In the house of Cornelius he perceives that God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation he that feareth him is accepted.
“In the estimation of God all men are equal.” The American Declaration held the truth self-evident in 1776, while most who signed it held slaves.
Justice Harlan, dissenting alone when the Supreme Court upheld segregated railway cars, said what the reading says of God’s justice about his country’s law: our Constitution is color-blind.
“Whosoever has a pure heart, his deeds are better.” The Qur’an: We made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another; the noblest of you in the sight of God is the best in conduct.

The reading lists what the two races share and asks for mutual consideration. Booker T. Washington offered the South a different bargain in 1895: in all things purely social separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in mutual progress. Can the hand be one while the fingers refuse to touch?
“Both are constituted alike and exist under the same law of growth.” Shylock argues from the same common body: hath not a Jew eyes? If you prick us, do we not bleed?
The races as clustered jewels of different kinds. Horace Kallen, opposing the melting pot in 1915, chose an orchestra: each instrument with its own timbre, the harmony made of their difference.

A bouquet of violets “in varying colors, dark and light”. Zangwill’s play of 1908 made America God’s crucible where the races melt and re-form. A bouquet keeps its colours; a crucible does not. Which picture do these readings draw?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá sees black and white seated together and takes it as evidence of “a just and free government”. Langston Hughes, a few years later: “They send me to eat in the kitchen / When company comes.” What did the assembly show, and what did it leave out?
The sixth candle makes of all peoples “kindreds of one race”. Zephaniah foresees the peoples turned to a pure language, to serve with one consent.

All are descendants of Adam, so racial distinction is “nothing but superstition”. The English rebels of 1381 drew the same conclusion about rank: when Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?

The reading rests one family on descent from Adam. Darwin came to a common descent by another road, and to differences of degree, not of kind. Does the conclusion need the genealogy, or stand without it?
Sheep of different colours graze together. Isaiah’s picture of peace goes further and puts the wolf beside the lamb.
Man is “the manifestation of divine bestowals”: shall racial ideas obscure the purpose? Genesis gives one origin and one dignity: in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
“Loosed from ancient superstitions.” Emerson opens Nature by asking why his age should grope among the dry bones of the past and not enjoy an original relation to the universe.
“Of every race and creed, members of one family.” Paul to Gentile converts: no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens, and of the household of God.
“There is no black and white in the Kingdom of God.” Paul’s sentence on the divisions of his own world: neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female.
The gates are open and no distinction remains. Jesus, marvelling at a Roman’s faith: many shall come from the east and west and sit down in the kingdom.
Believers in distant lands are “present in spirit and heart”. Paul to a church he had never seen: though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit.

A black man is praised as the pupil of the eye. Blake’s little black boy says “I am black, but O! my soul is white”: tenderness that still takes whiteness for the measure. How do the readings’ images of light and dark escape that, or do they?
A black believer shines in a meeting in Stuttgart. The first Gentile convert whose story Acts tells at length is an Ethiopian, a court official reading Isaiah in his chariot.

“Blackness is the darkness of the heart and not the darkness of the face.” Jeremiah’s proverb, can the Ethiopian change his skin, uses skin as the type of what cannot change. The reading turns it round: what must change is the heart, and can.

Hatred between black and white is to be healed by “the power of the Kingdom”. Frederick Douglass had seen religion on the other side: between the Christianity of this land and the Christianity of Christ he recognised the widest possible difference. What must religion be to heal what it had blessed?
“Intense is the hatred, in America.” Du Bois had written in 1903 that the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line.
“Surely man should not” quarrel over colour. Job on his servant: did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us?
Man, “so much higher in creation, should not be lower than the animals”. Marcus Aurelius asks himself constantly to regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul.

Race unifies only against outsiders and “does not blend people together”. Kipling’s ballad, so often quoted for its first line, ends by denying it: there is neither East nor West, Border, nor Breed, nor Birth, when two strong men stand face to face.
“Flimsy excuses” for war. Montaigne, hearing of the peoples of the New World, observed that every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country.

Remove racial, patriotic and religious prejudice, and people “will live in friendliness”. Kant doubted any such removal: out of the crooked timber of humanity no straight thing was ever made. Is prejudice a cause that can be removed, or a grain in the wood?
“The surface of the earth one place of residence.” Asked where he came from, Diogenes answered that he was a citizen of the world.

A Bahá’í is “free from all prejudices”. The Roman playwright Terence, born in Africa and brought to Rome a slave, wrote the line: I am a man, and nothing that concerns a man do I deem a matter of indifference to me.
“This enmity will increase day by day and … lead to bloodshed.” Lincoln in 1858, quoting the Gospel: a house divided against itself cannot stand.

The “downtrodden race” and the white are to be joined in serving the world. King from Birmingham jail: we are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality; whatever affects one directly affects all indirectly.

Kipling’s poem of 1899 speaks for the view the reading has to overcome: “Take up the White Man’s burden”, the peoples served being “half-devil and half-child”. The reading also speaks of raising a race. What separates its hope from his?
Jefferson, a slaveholder, had foreseen it: “I tremble for my country when I reflect that God is just; that his justice cannot sleep for ever.”

The reading notes how far the coloured people have advanced, and warns of war if the problem is not solved. Douglass: if there is no struggle there is no progress; power concedes nothing without a demand. What place has demand in the readings’ way of love?

The reading counts the “points of partnership and agreement” between the races. Donne’s meditation says why they outweigh the rest: no man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent.
“The names of black and white shall vanish. All shall be called human.” Burns sang it of rank: a man’s a man for a’ that, and man to man the world o’er shall brothers be.
“This is impossible except through love.” Paul’s chapter on charity makes the same thing the one indispensable gift.
Three meetings, until none could say which colour predominated. At Pentecost Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Cretes and Arabians each hear in their own tongue.
Friendly intercourse is possible even where law withholds equality. Paul sends a runaway slave back to his master with a letter: receive him not now as a servant, but a brother beloved.

“The whites in America fought four years” to free the slaves. Garrison’s Liberator had demanded it thirty years before the war, under a motto wider than the nation. He would not separate friendship from politics; the reading, for its hearers, does. Why?
Colours “are not the image and likeness of God”. James rebukes a congregation that seats the man in fine clothing well and tells the poor man to stand: are ye not partial in yourselves?
Climate, not worth, made the colours. Amos has God ask Israel: are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me? The chosen people are told they are one people among others He has led.
The Ethiopians descend from Shem and Ham alike. Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses “because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married”, and it is the complainers who are rebuked.
Five races, like the varieties of doves. Hopkins gives glory “for dappled things”, all things counter, original, spare, strange.
Having ended chattel slavery, “you must destroy industrial slavery”. Lincoln told Congress in 1861 that labor is prior to, and independent of, capital, and deserves much the higher consideration.
The Church’s hierarchy “has reversed Christ’s and Paul’s teaching of unity”. The text it reversed: be not ye called Rabbi; one is your Master, and all ye are brethren.

Hearts are “a blank scroll”. Mandela wrote from the other end of a long life in Africa: no one is born hating another because of the colour of his skin; people must learn to hate, and can be taught to love.

Mr. Gregory is to carry the message through the South, into churches, colleges and schools. Paul’s chain of questions: how shall they hear without a preacher? and how shall they preach, except they be sent?

The advice is that acceptance of the teachings will win “the confidence of the whites”. Du Bois describes the cost of always seeing oneself through the eyes of others: two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings in one dark body. Whose confidence has to be won?
“Are the colored and white believers entirely united?” John’s test of any claim to love God: he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?

Notables of the capital would not come if coloured people were present. George Washington had promised a synagogue that the government would give to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance; here the bigotry is social, and is refused at the door.
Some “protested” at love between white and black. Jesus answers a lawyer’s “who is my neighbour?” with a man of the despised race who showed mercy: go, and do thou likewise.
“Strive with heart and soul to create fellowship.” The new commandment: as I have loved you, that ye also love one another.
“Strive that intense love may be produced.” Paul describes what such love does when it meets resistance: it suffereth long, is not easily provoked, beareth all things.

They are to become “brethren reclining upon couches, face to face”, the Qur’an’s picture of paradise. King’s picture was the red hills of Georgia, where the sons of former slaves and of former slave owners sit down together at the table of brotherhood.
Gatherings of black and white manifest the oneness of humanity. The psalm: how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Such an assembly “becomes a magnet for the Concourse on High”. Jesus promises his presence where two or three are gathered in his name.
“The meeting is blessed” when the races meet in love. John sees a multitude no man could number, of all nations and kindreds and peoples and tongues, before the throne.
Eight singers, four white and four coloured, are “one of the great signs of God”. Paul: he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition.
White and coloured together “like unto the face and the hair of the Beloved”, and one voice raised. Paul asks his mixed congregations to teach one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.
Large meetings day and night, friendship made, “many came to the Faith”. The first church in Acts is described the same way: daily with one accord, having favour with all the people.
They “opened their home”. Job’s defence of his life includes this: the stranger did not lodge in the street, but I opened my doors to the traveller.
Meetings that establish friendship “among the world’s different races”. Isaiah: mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.

A convention in Washington, “because in that city there is great animosity”. Lincoln at Gettysburg dedicated the living to the unfinished work of a nation conceived in the proposition that all men are created equal.

A convention for the oneness of humanity “will become the cause of the removal of hostilities”. UNESCO’s founders put the principle in a sentence: since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.
“Thou must even endeavour that they intermarry.” Ruth the Moabite, marrying into Israel, says: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God. She becomes the great-grandmother of David.

Ezra, restoring a small people after exile, orders the opposite: separate yourselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wives. Scripture holds both Ruth and Ezra. What fear speaks in Ezra, and what answers it here?

A woman is persecuted for marrying a Japanese. Shakespeare’s Othello shows what such a marriage can meet: Iago, who says “I am not what I am”, works on a city’s prejudice until it destroys husband and wife. What must surround a marriage across races for it to be “a bond”?
In Bahá’í gatherings black and white “were like brothers and sisters”, and married. Paul grounds the same boldness in baptism: as many as have been baptized have put on Christ, and are all one.
The best fruit comes when one kind is grafted on another. Paul uses the gardener’s image for the joining of peoples: wild olive branches grafted in among the natural ones, partaking of the root.

A newspaper’s first duty is “creating harmony”. Jefferson trusted the press for another reason: error of opinion may be tolerated where reason is left free to combat it. Is a press that aims at harmony still free to report the quarrel?
Every student should know “that he is the brother of the people of all religions and nations”. A disciple of Confucius consoles a man without brothers: all within the four seas will be his brothers.
To look past colours to “the reality of humanity”. Tagore prays for a country where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls.
Unity between coloured and white “will be an assurance of the world’s peace”. Isaiah’s nations beat their swords into plowshares and learn war no more.
What was “impossible and unattainable” is done by the breaths of the Holy Spirit. Zechariah: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
After Christ, nations and tribes gathered “under the shadow of His Word”. Paul lists them: Greek, Jew, Barbarian, Scythian, bond, free.
“The Jew and the Muslim will blend together.” Genesis has one scene of it: Isaac and Ishmael, the estranged brothers, together bury their father Abraham.
“Here am I a Persian, and you an American.” Whitman saw God’s purpose from the first in the earth spanned and the races, neighbours, to marry and be given in marriage.
“It is just like a miracle, our being here together”, with no tie of race or country. Acts tells of a morning when they were all with one accord in one place.
The German will say “I am a Frenchman”, and the peoples will refuse war. Micah: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, and every man shall sit under his vine and fig tree.
“No blacks, no whites; both as one.” Paul: we, being many, are one body, and every one members one of another.
Love among all religions, and all races embracing. Micah’s vision of peace adds a line often passed over: all people will walk every one in the name of his god. Does embracing require becoming alike?

shortfall: Many readings repeat one statement in nearly the same words (that colour has no importance and the heart is what matters, that doves and sheep do not quarrel over colour, that a meeting of the two races is blessed); a companion was given to each form of the thought, not to each repetition.

colossians-neither-greek-nor-jew.text: Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all
